title: Distributed Sensor Aggregation for Smart Grids
business: A regional smart grid operator managing thousands of remote energy sensors.
problem: Individual sensor nodes frequently lose connectivity or crash due to environmental interference, causing cascading failures in the central monitoring system.
solution: Utilizing Erlang/OTP processes, the system isolates each sensor connection into a lightweight, independent process. By employing supervision trees, the system detects process termination and automatically restarts failed handlers, ensuring that a single sensor crash does not impact the broader grid monitoring capability.
steps: Define a supervisor process to monitor worker processes assigned to specific sensor IDs.
Implement worker processes using gen_server to handle incoming telemetry data via asynchronous message passing.
Configure restart strategies within the supervisor to handle transient network errors.
Use link or monitor primitives to establish fault-tolerant relationships between the supervisor and worker nodes.
outcome: The monitoring system achieves high availability where individual sensor failures are contained and recovered without manual intervention or system-wide downtime.
limitation: The primary trade-off is memory overhead; while Erlang processes are lightweight, spawning millions of processes for high-frequency granular data can lead to significant heap consumption. You can check this by monitoring the process count and memory usage via the erlang:memory/0 function.

questions.question: In Distributed Sensor Aggregation for Smart Grids, what is a potential limitation of the proposed architecture?
options: The system cannot handle more than ten sensors simultaneously.
Excessive memory usage if too many processes are spawned for granular data.
The system requires manual restarts for every sensor failure.
Erlang processes are too heavy to be used for network communication.
